mainTopic: Tenant-farming deals and the 'just a name' argument, and sages who drew laws from the everyday wording of documents (לשון הדיוט).
overview: The amud opens with the last line of a discussion from the previous daf: the owner tells the tenant he should have brought water in a bucket. רב פפא then gives a rule for reading the chapter. The first two משניות fit both a חוכר (fixed rent) and a מקבל (share of the crop). From the third משנה on, each case fits only one of them. The גמרא asks why a tenant who asked for 'this irrigated field' gets a rent reduction when the water dries up. A ברייתא shows that a seller can say 'I only told you the field's name.' שמואל answers that it depends on who described the field. רבינא answers that the word 'this' makes 'irrigated' a real promise. A new משנה rules that a tenant who leaves the field unworked must pay what it could have grown, because his contract says so. The גמרא explains that this follows sages who drew laws from the everyday wording of documents (לשון הדיוט): רבי מאיר, רבי יהודה, הלל הזקן and רבי יהושע בן קרחה, each with an example. Finally, the גמרא challenges רבי יהושע בן קרחה's case with a ruling of רבי יוחנן about collateral, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: You should have brought water in a bucket
steps.stepSummary: The closing line of the previous discussion: the landowner tells the tenant he should have brought water by bucket.
steps.simpleTranslation: You should have brought water in a bucket.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes a discussion from the previous daf. The landowner answers the tenant's complaint about the water by saying, 'You should have carried water in a bucket.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner's point is that the tenant could still have watered the field by hand. So the tenant cannot use the loss of the water source as a reason to pay less rent. With this answer, the earlier back-and-forth is closed.

keyTerms.meaning: You should have; it was up to you to
To bring
A bucket for drawing water

phrases.english: You should have brought water in a bucket.
phrases.notes: This is the landowner speaking to the tenant, finishing an argument that started on the previous daf.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבְּעִי לָךְ לְאֵתוֹיֵי בְּדַוְולָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion carried over from the previous daf.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical alternative: the tenant had another way to water the field.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tenant does not get a reduction, because he could have watered the field by bucket.

steps.title: רב פפא's map of the chapter
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the first two משניות apply to both kinds of tenant. From the third משנה on, each case fits only one kind.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: You can apply these first two משניות both to a fixed-rent tenant and to a share-tenant. From here on, what fits a share-tenant does not fit a fixed-rent tenant, and what fits a fixed-rent tenant does not fit a share-tenant.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a general guide for reading the chapter. The first two משניות fit both kinds of tenant, but the later ones each fit only one kind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חוכר pays the owner a set amount of produce no matter how the harvest turns out. A מקבל pays a fixed share, like a third or a quarter. Many later rules depend on which deal it is, so רב פפא tells us to read each later משנה as speaking about only one of them.

keyTerms.meaning: Fixed-rent tenancy: the tenant pays a set amount of produce
Share-tenancy: the tenant pays a set share, like a third or a quarter
From here on
It does not apply; it is not there

steps.whatToRemember: משניות 1-2 of the chapter fit both kinds of tenant. From משנה 3 on, each case fits either the חוכר or the מקבל, not both.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two kinds of tenant. In a חכירות deal the tenant owes a fixed amount; in a קבלנות deal he owes a share of whatever grows.

phrases.english: what applies in share-tenancy does not apply in fixed-rent tenancy,

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first two משניות fit both kinds of tenant. Each later משנה fits only one.

steps.title: Why can't the owner say he only used the name?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a tenant who asked for 'this irrigated field.' It asks why the owner cannot say the word 'irrigated' was only the field's name.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'If he said to him, Lease me this irrigated field...' (then he may take money off the rent if the water dries up). But why? Let the owner say to him: I only told you the name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings up a new line of the משנה and challenges its ruling. Why should the tenant get to pay less? The owner could say, 'Calling it irrigated was just its name, not a promise.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the משנה, the tenant's words 'this irrigated field' turn the water into part of the deal. The גמרא suggests that such a description might only be a label for the type of field. If so, the owner never promised that water would keep flowing. The proof for this idea comes in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: An irrigated field that needs watering
But why?
Just a name; only a label
Lease me (as a fixed-rent tenant)

phrases.english: If he said to him

phrases.aramaic: חֲכוֹר לִי שְׂדֵה בֵּית הַשְּׁלָחִין זֶה [וְכוּ׳].
phrases.english: 'Lease me this irrigated field,' etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה. It goes on: 'or this field of trees.' If the spring dried up or the trees were cut down, the tenant may take money off his rent.

phrases.english: But why?
Let him say to him:
phrases.notes: The owner is speaking to the tenant.

phrases.english: I merely told you the name,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַמַּאי? לֵימָא לֵיהּ: שְׁמָא בְּעָלְמָא אֲמַרִי לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next משנה in the order described by רב פפא and challenges its ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the tenant may take money off his rent when the water source dries up.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Describing the field as 'irrigated' may just be naming its type. If so, the owner made no promise, and there is no reason to lower the rent.

steps.title: A 'בית כור' sold by name only
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא is brought as support: someone sold a field called a 'בית כור' that was really only half that size, and the sale still stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it taught in a ברייתא: If someone says to his friend, 'I am selling you a בית כור of land,' even though it holds only a לתך, the sale stands, because he only sold him a name. This is so when the field is known as a 'בית כור.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show that the 'just a name' argument really works. A seller who called a field a 'בית כור' does not have to deliver that full size.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בית כור is a large measure of land, and a לתך is only half of it. The buyer still cannot cancel the sale. That is because 'בית כור' was simply what people call this field, not a promise about its size. The rule holds only when the field really is commonly known by that name.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it taught in a ברייתא?
An area of land big enough to sow a כור of seed
Half a כור
Literally 'it reached him': the sale stands
That it is called

phrases.english: Isn't it taught:
One who says to his fellow
'I am selling you a beit kor of land,'

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ אֶלָּא לֶתֶךְ –
phrases.english: even though it contains only a half-kor –
it is his
phrases.notes: The buyer keeps the field and can't back out of the sale.

phrases.english: for he sold him only a name,
and that is when it is called a 'beit kor.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי לָא תַּנְיָא: הָאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ

steps.raayaObject: That a seller can say 'I only gave you the name.'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about selling a field called a 'בית כור' that holds only a לתך.

steps.title: Vineyard without vines, orchard without pomegranates
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues with two more cases: a 'vineyard' with no vines and an 'orchard' with no pomegranates. Both sales stand.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'I am selling you a vineyard': even though it has no vines, the sale stands, because he only sold him a name, and this is when it is called a 'vineyard.' 'I am selling you an orchard': even though it has no pomegranates, the sale stands, because he only sold him a name, and this is when it is called an 'orchard.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא repeats the same rule for two more kinds of field. Each time, the field's name is not a promise about what is growing on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These cases are even closer to the משנה's case than the size case. Here the name ('vineyard,' 'orchard') describes what the field is used for, much like 'irrigated field.' Still, the seller owes nothing beyond the name.

keyTerms.meaning: A vineyard
Grapevines
An orchard
Pomegranates

phrases.english: even though it has no vines – it is his,
for he sold him only a name,

phrases.english: even though it has no pomegranates – it is his,

steps.raayaObject: That a name describing what a field is used for is not a promise.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The rest of the ברייתא: the vineyard and orchard cases.

steps.title: So the owner should be able to say 'just a name' here too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws the lesson from the ברייתא: a seller can say 'I only told you the name,' so the landowner in our משנה should be able to say the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: So we see that he can say to him: I only told you the name. Here too, let him say to him: I only told you the name!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge. If the 'just a name' answer works for a seller, it should also work for the landowner in our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא shows that calling a field by its usual name is not a promise. 'Irrigated field' looks just like 'vineyard' or 'orchard.' So it is hard to see why the משנה lets the tenant take money off the rent. The גמרא now needs an answer that explains the difference.

keyTerms.meaning: So we see; apparently
Here too; the same way

phrases.english: So we see he can say to him:
I merely told you the name.
So too here, let him say to him:
I merely told you the name!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא אָמַר לֵיהּ: שְׁמָא בְּעָלְמָא אֲמַרִי לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the rule from the ברייתא and applies it to the משנה, completing the challenge from step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a tenant of an 'irrigated field' may take money off his rent.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא shows that a field's name is not a promise. The landowner should be able to use that same answer.

steps.title: It depends on who described the field
steps.stepSummary: שמואל answers that the ברייתא is about an owner who described the field, while our משנה is about a tenant who asked for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: There is no difficulty. In the ברייתא the owner said it to the tenant. In the משנה the tenant said it to the owner. When the owner says it, he was just using the field's name. When the tenant says it, he really cared about it.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the challenge from Step 6 by showing that the ברייתא and our משנה are talking about two different speakers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner (מחכיר) can describe his field loosely, and the label is just a name. But when the tenant (חוכר) asks for 'this irrigated field,' he is stating what he wants, so 'irrigated' is a real condition. That is why the tenant may take money off his rent when the water dries up.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction
The landowner who rents out the field
The tenant who rents the field for a fixed payment
Just a name, with no real promise behind it
Being particular; really caring about a detail

phrases.english: Shmuel said: It is not difficult:
This is where the owner said it to the tenant,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the ברייתא about selling a field with a misleading name.

phrases.english: that is where the tenant said it to the owner.
phrases.notes: 'That' is our משנה, where the tenant asked for 'this irrigated field.'

phrases.english: If the owner said it to the tenant,
he just told him a name.
If the tenant said it to the owner, it shows he was particular about it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל, לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 6 by splitting the cases according to who spoke.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different cases: who said the words
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא and the משנה are the same kind of case, so the owner should be able to say 'it was just a name.'
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the owner's own description can be 'just a name.' A tenant who asks for an irrigated field cares about it, so it is a real condition.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that the same words can carry different weight depending on who says them and why.

steps.title: The word 'this' shows they stood in the field
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says the owner spoke in both cases. But since he said 'this' field, they were standing in it, so 'irrigated' must mean it will stay irrigated as it is now.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: In both cases the owner said it to the tenant. But since he said 'this,' we must be talking about someone standing inside the field. So why did he need to say 'irrigated'? Because he meant: an irrigated field just as it is right now.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives a different answer to the same challenge. He looks closely at the word 'this' in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If they were standing in the field, the tenant could already see it was irrigated. So the word 'irrigated' was not needed as a name. It must be a promise that the field will stay watered as it is now. In the ברייתא there was no 'this,' so the label could just be a name.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this and that; both cases
From this we can infer
An irrigated field, watered by channels
As it stands now

steps.confusionAlert: רבינא does not argue with the rule that a seller can say 'it was just a name.' He only shows that in our משנה the word 'irrigated' was extra, so it must mean something real.
steps.whatToRemember: Two answers: שמואל says it depends on who spoke. רבינא says the owner spoke both times, but 'this' plus 'irrigated' together make a real promise that the field stays as it is now.

phrases.english: Ravina said: Both this and that
are where the owner said it to the tenant.
Since he said 'this,'
we can infer that we are dealing with someone standing inside it.
Why does he need to say 'irrigated field'?

just as it stands now.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the same קשיא, different from שמואל's.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the wording of the משנה closely
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the owner spoke, 'irrigated' could be just the field's name, like in the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word 'this' shows they were in the field, so 'irrigated' was not needed as a name. It must be a promise to keep the field as it is now.

steps.title: A tenant who leaves the field unworked must pay
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: if a tenant takes a field and does not work it, the court estimates what it could have grown, and he pays the owner, because his contract says so.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone who receives a field from his friend and leaves it unplanted: we estimate how much it could have produced, and he pays the owner. Because this is what he writes to him: 'If I leave it unplanted and do not work it, I will pay from the best.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches that a tenant cannot just leave the field idle and pay nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner was counting on his share of the crops. Even if nothing grew because the tenant did nothing, the court figures out what should have grown, and the tenant pays that. The reason given is the standard wording of the tenant's contract.

keyTerms.meaning: A sharecropper who works the field for a share of the crops
He left it unplanted
We estimate the value
From the best quality

phrases.english: Mishnah: One who receives a field from his friend and leaves it unplanted,
we estimate how much it was able to produce,
and he gives it to him.
phrases.notes: The tenant pays the owner the owner's share of that estimated crop.

phrases.english: For this is what he writes to him:
'If I leave it unplanted and do not work it,'
'I will pay from the best.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַמְקַבֵּל שָׂדֶה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ וְהוֹבִירָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of the irrigated field is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tenant who leaves the field unworked pays the owner what it could have produced, based on his contract.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a contract's standard wording can create a real obligation to pay.

steps.title: רבי מאיר learned laws from everyday wording
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the משנה follows רבי מאיר, who drew laws from the plain wording ordinary people wrote in their documents.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רבי מאיר used to explain the language of ordinary people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by telling us whose approach the משנה follows. This sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally laws come from the תורה or the חכמים. רבי מאיר also took the regular wording people used in their contracts seriously, and drew rulings from it. That is why the משנה relies on the contract line 'I will pay from the best.'

keyTerms.meaning: Explains and draws a lesson from
The language of ordinary people, such as in their contracts

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ רַבִּי מֵאִיר הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן הֶדְיוֹט.
phrases.english: Gemara: Rabbi Meir would explain the language of ordinary people.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן הֶדְיוֹט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the משנה's reliance on the contract wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר drew laws from the everyday wording people used in their documents.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows רבי מאיר used the contract wording
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא is quoted where רבי מאיר relies on the line 'If I leave it unplanted and do not work it, I will pay from the best.'
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: רבי מאיר says: 'If I leave it unplanted and do not work it, I will pay from the best.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove what it just said about רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, רבי מאיר makes the tenant pay because of this exact contract line. This shows he draws a ruling from the everyday wording of the document, just like our משנה does.

keyTerms.meaning: I will leave it unplanted
I will work it

phrases.english: As it was taught: Rabbi Meir says:

steps.title: רבי יהודה also learned from everyday wording
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds that רבי יהודה, like רבי מאיר, drew laws from the plain wording people wrote.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה used to learn laws from the everyday language people used.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names a second sage who learned from everyday wording. It is setting up a ברייתא that will prove this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 said רבי מאיר was דורש לשון הדיוט. Now the גמרא shows this was not only his approach. רבי יהודה did the same, and a source is about to be brought.

keyTerms.meaning: Learns out, draws a law from

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן הֶדְיוֹט.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda would expound common language.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן הֶדְיוֹט

steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה also derived laws from the wording of ordinary documents.

steps.title: A husband pays for his wife's offerings because of the כתובה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: רבי יהודה rules that a husband brings the rich man's קרבן for his wife and pays for all her קרבנות, because the כתובה says he takes on her obligations, even ones from before.
steps.simpleTranslation: As taught in a ברייתא, רבי יהודה says: A man brings the offering of a rich person for his wife, and the same goes for every offering she must bring. This is because he writes her a guarantee: 'what you have upon me, from before this.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that רבי יהודה learned from everyday wording. He bases a law about קרבנות on a line in the כתובה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband's wealth decides which version of the קרבן his wife brings, and he must pay for all her קרבנות. The reason is not a פסוק. It is the line in the כתובה where he accepts her obligations, even ones from before. That is exactly learning from לשון הדיוט.

keyTerms.meaning: The more expensive version of an offering, brought by someone who can afford it
A guarantee, a responsibility the husband accepts
From before this, meaning obligations from earlier

phrases.english: A man brings the offering of a rich person on behalf of his wife,
phrases.notes: Some offerings cost less for a poor person. Here the husband's money counts, even if the wife herself has none.

phrases.english: and likewise every single offering that she is obligated to bring,
because this is how he writes her a guarantee:

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִית לִיךְ עֲלַי מִן קַדְמַת דְּנָא.
phrases.english: 'That which you have, is upon me, even from before this.'
phrases.notes: This is the Aramaic line from the כתובה. He takes on her debts, even ones from before the marriage.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source proving the claim in step 12.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה was דורש לשון הדיוט.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where רבי יהודה bases the husband's duty to pay for his wife's קרבנות on the wording of the כתובה.

steps.title: הלל הזקן also learned from everyday wording
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא names הלל הזקן as another sage who learned from the wording of ordinary documents.
steps.simpleTranslation: הלל the Elder used to learn laws from the everyday language people used.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a third sage to the list. It is setting up a ברייתא with a story about הלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same claim made about רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה. The story that follows will show how הלל used it to decide a serious question.

phrases.aramaic: הִלֵּל הַזָּקֵן הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן הֶדְיוֹט,
phrases.english: Hillel the Elder would expound common language,

steps.triggerLanguage: הִלֵּל הַזָּקֵן הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן הֶדְיוֹט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of sages who were דורש לשון הדיוט.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הלל הזקן also derived laws from the wording of ordinary documents.

steps.title: The problem in Alexandria: brides snatched before the חופה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא tells that in Alexandria, women who had קידושין were snatched by other men on the way to the חופה. The חכמים wanted to rule that their children were ממזרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: As taught in a ברייתא: The people of Alexandria would betroth their wives. When the women were entering the חופה, other men would come and snatch them away. The חכמים wanted to declare their children ממזרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins the ברייתא about הלל by laying out the problem. The solution comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After קידושין a woman counts as married. So children she has with another man would normally be ממזרים. That is why the חכמים wanted to rule this way.

keyTerms.meaning: Betroth, perform קידושין, the first stage of marriage
The wedding canopy, the second stage of marriage
Snatch, grab away
Children from a forbidden union, such as a married woman with another man

phrases.english: As it is taught: The people of Alexandria
would betroth their wives,
and at the time they were entering the wedding canopy,
others would come and snatch them away from them,
and the Sages wanted to make their children mamzerim.
phrases.notes: "Their children" means the children these women later had with the men who snatched them.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: אַנְשֵׁי אֲלֶכְּסַנְדְּרִיָּא הָיוּ מְקַדְּשִׁין אֶת נְשׁוֹתֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the ברייתא that proves step 14 by presenting the case.
steps.raayaObject: That הלל הזקן was דורש לשון הדיוט.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about the brides of Alexandria (the setup part).

steps.title: הלל reads the כתובה and saves the children
steps.stepSummary: הלל asks for the mothers' כתובה. It says 'When you enter the חופה, be my wife,' so the marriage never took effect, and the children are not ממזרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: הלל the Elder said to them: 'Bring me your mother's כתובה.' They brought it, and he found written in it: 'When you enter the חופה, be my wife.' So they did not declare their children ממזרים.
steps.whatsHappening: הלל solves the problem by reading the exact words of the כתובה. This finishes the proof that he learned from everyday wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'when you enter the חופה' make the marriage start only at the חופה. These women never got there, so they were never fully married. Their children from the other men are therefore not ממזרים, all based on the plain wording of the document.

keyTerms.meaning: The marriage contract
When you will enter
As a wife (Aramaic)

steps.whatToRemember: הלל ruled from the exact words of the כתובה: the marriage depended on entering the חופה. Since that never happened, the children were not ממזרים.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think הלל cancelled the law of ממזרות. He just showed from the wording that these women were never fully married, so the law never applied.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how strong לשון הדיוט can be. The exact words people write can decide even a very serious issue like personal status.

phrases.english: Hillel the Elder said to them:
phrases.notes: "Them" is the children whose status was in question.

phrases.english: Bring me your mother's marriage contract.
They brought him their mother's marriage contract,
and he found that it was written in it:
'When you enter the wedding canopy, be my wife.'
And they did not make their children mamzerim.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן הִלֵּל הַזָּקֵן: הָבִיאוּ לִי כְּתוּבַּת אִמְּכֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the problem set up in step 15 and completes the proof for step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That הלל הזקן was דורש לשון הדיוט.
steps.raayaSupportSource: הלל's ruling based on the wording 'when you enter the חופה, be my wife' in the כתובה.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן קרחה also learned from everyday wording
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא names רבי יהושע בן קרחה as a fourth sage who learned from the wording of ordinary documents.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן קרחה used to learn laws from the everyday language people used.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more sage to the list. It is setting up a ברייתא about loans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same pattern as before: first the claim, then the source. The source this time is about a משכון, collateral taken for a loan.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן הֶדְיוֹט.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha would expound common language.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן הֶדְיוֹט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of sages who were דורש לשון הדיוט.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע בן קרחה also derived laws from the wording of ordinary documents.

steps.title: A lender may not take collateral worth more than the debt
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: רבי יהושע בן קרחה rules that a lender may not take a משכון worth more than the loan, because the document says the payment is equal to this item.
steps.simpleTranslation: As taught in a ברייתא, רבי יהושע בן קרחה says: One who lends to his fellow may not take collateral worth more than the debt. This is because he writes to him: 'The payment you have upon me is against all of this.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that רבי יהושע בן קרחה learned from everyday wording. He bases a law about collateral on the wording of the loan document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The document says the debt corresponds to 'all of this,' meaning the item taken. That wording shows the item should be worth the same as the debt. So the lender may not hold more than the debt is worth.

keyTerms.meaning: One who lends money
Take collateral (a משכון) from him
The payment (Aramaic)
Against all of this, equal to this item

steps.whatToRemember: Four sages were דורש לשון הדיוט: רבי מאיר, רבי יהודה, הלל הזקן and רבי יהושע בן קרחה. Each drew a law from the exact wording ordinary people wrote in their documents.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says:
One who lends money to his fellow
may not take collateral from him worth more than his debt,
because this is what he writes to him:
'The payment that you have upon me
is equal to all of this.'
phrases.notes: "This" is the collateral item. The debt and the item are meant to match in value.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source proving the claim in step 17.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהושע בן קרחה was דורש לשון הדיוט.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא limiting collateral to the value of the debt, based on the document's wording 'כל קבל דיכי'.

steps.title: Inference: the lender owns the collateral only because it was written
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers from רבי יהושע בן קרחה's teaching that the lender owns the collateral only because the document says so. Without that wording, he would not own it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason the lender owns the collateral is that the document says so. That implies that if it did not say so, he would not own it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is reading closely into the previous ברייתא and pulling out a hidden implication. This is a setup line that prepares for a challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן קרחה based his ruling on the wording of the document, which treats the collateral as equal to the payment. The גמרא concludes that this wording is the reason the lender owns the collateral. So without the wording, the lender should have no ownership.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason
But if not. This introduces the opposite case that follows from the reason.
He acquires it, he becomes the owner

phrases.english: The reason is that he wrote this to him,
phrases.notes: 'This' means the line from the last step: the payment is equal to this item.

phrases.aramaic: הָא אִי לָא כְּתַב לֵיהּ הָכִי –
phrases.english: but if he did not write this to him –
he would not acquire it?

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דִּכְתַב לֵיהּ הָכִי, הָא אִי לָא כְּתַב לֵיהּ הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from רבי יהושע בן קרחה's ruling in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tentative inference, raised only so the next step can challenge it: it would seem a lender owns the collateral only if the document says so.

steps.title: Challenge from רבי יוחנן: the lender owns collateral even without wording
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules on a specific case. A lender took collateral, then gave it back, and then the borrower died. The lender can still take it from the borrower's children. This shows the lender owns collateral even without any special wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי יוחנן said: if a lender took collateral, gave it back to the borrower, and the borrower died, the lender takes it away from the borrower's children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the inference from the last step using a ruling of רבי יוחנן. That ruling suggests a lender automatically owns collateral, even with no document wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן lets the lender take the collateral back from the borrower's children, even though the lender had already returned it. This only makes sense if the collateral already counts as the lender's property. If that ownership comes automatically, then the wording רבי יהושע בן קרחה relied on should not be needed.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? This opens a challenge from an outside source.
He took collateral from him
And he returned it to him
He pulls it away, he takes it back

steps.confusionAlert: Don't get confused by the order of events here. The lender gave the collateral back before the borrower died, yet he can still take it from the children.
steps.whyThisMatters: It raises a basic question: does taking collateral give the lender ownership automatically, or only when the document gives it to him?

phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Yoḥanan say:
If he took collateral from him and returned the collateral to him,
and he died – he takes it away from his children.
phrases.notes: 'He died' means the borrower. 'He takes it away' means the lender takes it back.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference made in step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that a lender owns the collateral only when the document says so.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן says the lender can take returned collateral back from the borrower's children, so the collateral already counts as his. That shows ownership comes without any wording.
